metadata.note: The Michigan Central's Michigan network beyond its Detroit-Chicago main line (michigan_central_detroit_chicago.geojson) and its Jackson-Bay City Saginaw Division (michigan_central_lansing_saginaw.geojson). The centrepiece is the northern half of the Jackson, Lansing & Saginaw -- the Central's route to the Straits of Mackinac. The JL&S was leased by the Michigan Central in 1871, reached Gaylord in July 1873, and was completed from Jackson all the way to Mackinaw City on December 31 1881; it merged into the Michigan Central in 1916 and was run as the Mackinaw Division. Around it: the Detroit & Bay City (Detroit-Oxford 1872, through to Bay City July 31 1873, MC control 1875 and outright 1881); the Grand River Valley (Jackson-Grand Rapids, opened 1870 and leased to the MC for 999 years the same year); the Toledo, Canada Southern & Detroit (Detroit-Toledo, built 1873, MC operating agreement 1882); and three branches the Central picked up in the 1880s and 1890s -- the Saginaw Bay & Northwestern (1884), the St. Louis, Sturgis & Battle Creek (1889) and the Grayling, Twin Lakes & Northeastern (1891).
sources: https://michiganrailroads.com/railroads-in-history/462-i-j/3520-jackson-lansing-and-saginaw-railroad-company (JL&S completed Jackson-Lansing and Owosso-Saginaw/Bay City, extended to Gaylord July 1873, entire Jackson-Mackinaw City line completed December 31 1881; leased to Michigan Central 1871, merged 1916; MC paid $70,750 annual rental)

https://michiganrailroads.com/railroads-in-history/459-d/3405-detroit-bay-city-railroad (Detroit & Bay City opened Bay City Junction to Oxford 1872, completed Detroit to Bay City July 31 1873, about 110 miles; Michigan Central control 1875, took over 1881)

https://www.michiganrailroads.com/railroads-in-history/461-g-h/3487-grand-river-valley-railroad-company (Grand River Valley Railroad, Jackson to Grand Rapids, opened 1870, 83.79 miles of main line plus 17.01 miles of sidings and spurs; leased for 999 years to the Michigan Central in 1870)

https://michiganrailroads.com/railroads-in-history/486-t-v/7991-toledo-canada-southern-and-detroit-railway (company formed 1872; line built from Peninsular Junction through Grand Junction in Detroit to Toledo in 1873; Michigan Central operating agreement and takeover 1882)

https://michiganrailroads.com/railroads-in-history/464-m/3841-michigan-central-railroad (Michigan Central acquisitions: Saginaw Bay & Northwestern 1884, St. Louis, Sturgis & Battle Creek 1889; control of the Grayling, Twin Lakes & Northeastern 1891)
geometry_sources: Wikimedia Commons Data:Michigan Central Railroad.map (CC BY 4.0), linked from the New York Central Railroad article's system map and itself derived from OpenStreetMap. The Mackinaw Division feature is the Commons 'Jackson, Lansing and Saginaw Railroad' LineString split at Bay City; the southern remainder was used to correct michigan_central_lansing_saginaw.geojson. All features were checked with the place-anchor artifact detector and came back clean.

Length checks against the sources: Bay City-Mackinaw City traces at 293.8 km (182.6 miles) against a documented route of about 180 miles; Grand River Valley at 136.5 km (84.8 miles) against a documented 83.79 miles.

Straight-line chords remain where the source geometry is sparse: up to 7.7 km on the Detroit & Bay City, 7.4 km on the Toledo, Canada Southern & Detroit, 5.5 km on the St. Louis, Sturgis & Battle Creek and 3.8 km on the Grand River Valley.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: All headways are estimated. Opening dates for the St. Louis, Sturgis & Battle Creek, Grayling, Twin Lakes & Northeastern and Saginaw Bay & Northwestern are not sourced -- those features begin at the documented Michigan Central acquisition or control date instead. No passenger-service end date is sourced for any feature here; all are modelled to the 1968 Penn Central merger, which is certainly too late for the rural branches.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
